text: Sunday morning, Mok is on every channel in handcuffs: attempted murder, on a stream two point one million people watched.
Black Hound loses its licence, and its big dog's-head sign comes down.
And Kanghan buries Black Hound in one sentence. Mok was a contractor acting alone.
In the corner store, the radish granny glares at the TV. Acting alone, her foot.
Jaeha has been asleep for seventeen hours, the cat on his chest. Let him sleep, Nib says. He carried every hit.
Then his phone buzzes. Inspector Ryu, from the Association.
The core is evidence now. Jaeha's share waits for the trial. Of course, sir. Thank you, sir.
Lyra spins round. The nine hundred million: what's her cut? Jaeha's answer: evidence.
Lyra flops back in despair. This world is stupid.
Then Seoa smacks her brother with a pillow and won't let go of his sleeve. He almost died on live TV, and she was watching.
That afternoon, Jaeha limps into a quiet columbarium on a walking stick, Nib at his side.
Behind one small glass door: an urn, a can of coffee, a tiny wooden husk, and a photo of Minseok, grinning, thumbs up.
Jaeha takes off his cap. Hi, hyung. Sorry it took four years.
He presses a thumbs-up sticker onto the glass, the same one as on the phone.
Was he strong, Nib asks. No. He was F-rank too. He just always went first.
Nib lifts his mask to see the photo with his own eyes. He would have liked him.
Then Choi walks up with two cans of coffee. Minseok took his with three sugars. Disgusting.
Jaeha had no idea. Choi comes every year on the day, at lunch. Jaeha comes at night.
He holds out an old USB stick. The phone is in an evidence locker. This isn't.
Jaeha takes it like it might break. But hyung never came out. So how did Mok have his phone?
Choi remembers a Black Hound man helping him carry Jaeha off that door. He went through Jaeha's vest. Looking for core shards, he said.
The colour drains out of Jaeha's eyes.
Four years ago, in grey: a screaming young Jaeha carried from the iron door, and young Mok's hand slipping an orange phone out of his pocket.
Jaeha presses a hand to his chest. Minseok put it in his pocket when he pushed him out. It was for him.
Choi pats his shoulder. It took four years, but it got to him. And he's bringing kimbap tonight.
Jaeha and Nib stand in the sunlight beside the little sticker.
That evening, everyone is on the rooftop around a huge pan of tteokbokki.
Borro presents his first harvest: a crate of lettuce, for the team.
Nib won't touch it until someone else tastes it. It's lettuce, says Seoa. Exactly what a poisoner would say.
Seoa tries it. It's really good.
Nib then eats half the crate.
Bomi leaps up screaming. BomBom TV just hit a million subscribers.
Saturday's stream peaked at two million, and the donations came to over forty-eight million won.
Four shares, she says: Jaeha, Bomi, Yerin, and the husks. No arguing. It's already sent.
Just over twenty-four million won lands in Jaeha's account.
Lyra is delighted. Finally, someone in this world understands money.
The school trip, Seoa reads, and the rent for a whole year. The landlady relents. Fine. The pets can stay.
Nib, lettuce hanging from his mouth, is not a pet.
On the water tank, Lyra lounges against the dusk sky with a bottle of soju. The drink is terrible. Pour her another.
Jaeha looks very hard in the other direction. Nib stares at him.
Then she sits beside him, serious. When do they look for Ilan? Soon, he promises. Humans promise a lot.
Yerin tells him shyly she didn't freeze this time. He knows. He was on her back.
Jaeha looks around at all of them. Everyone came back. Every single one.
Late at night, the party is over. Borro sleeps by his garden, the cat on his shell.
Across the city, a gloved hand flicks a silver baton.
In the Kanghan guild hall, a woman in white conducts forty white husks alone, all in perfect step, and owns every inch of the floor.
Her tablet shows an expense: a Han River site, maintenance surveys, five trap-testers, paid weekly in cash.
Maintenance surveys, she whispers. On a Han River gate they don't have.
Forty husks lower their arms as one, and she looks out toward the river.
Two forty-seven a.m. Lyra snores on the floor, rolled up like a burrito, while Jaeha sits at the laptop with Choi's USB stick.
He drags the video past the moment the phone died.
And Minseok keeps talking. Eat something, kid. You never eat.
He glances behind the phone. Okay. This is where we are. Just in case.
The camera swings round.
Through the shimmer of the gate's rim: a bridge pier on the Han, a faded yellow seven, and one cracked lamp.
Jaeha doesn't blink.
He's seen that pier through Nib's eyes, four years later, with a gate glowing under it and cables round its rim.
The gate under the bridge, he whispers. Pier seven, Nib whispers back. With the broken lamp. That's it.
But the official record says that gate closed four years ago. Boss cleared.
Closed, Nib reads. And yet he saw it open with his own eyes.
Every child in this world knows the rule. A gate only closes when its boss dies.
Jaeha crosses out Mok in his notebook and writes underneath: pier seven. Still open. So its boss is still alive.
Four years. Somebody has been keeping it alive.
From the parapet, he looks toward a bridge two kilometres away, and the cold glow under one pier. Your gate is still open, hyung.
And far away under the bridge, the glow pulses once, slowly, like a heartbeat.
